## Part 1 · 00:02

[00:02] So, what name should be used when referring to God or Jesus? I see a lot of comments and posts from people saying things like, "You shouldn't use the name Jesus or Jehovah because there was no J back then and that's not really his name." They'll say, "It's Yahweh." And then I see other people saying it's Yeshua, but some will still say Jehovah versus Jesus. And really, everyone just has their own opinion on what is acceptable for them.

[00:34] It's true that the letter J wasn't introduced into the English language until the 1600s and it was particularly used in a Cambridge edition of the King James Bible where it replaced the I for J's for names like Jesus or James. And although the letter J was recognized as a letter in 1524, even the 1611 version of the King James Bible still used I instead of J. But I think it's important to realize that these names are just translations or cultural iterations of the same thing.

[01:02] Different cultures will spell and pronounce a city name or a person's name just a little bit differently based on their own language, but they're all talking about the same person or place. But the question is, do we really know what God's name is? We aren't really told specifically. In the Old Testament, there is this being called the name. It is a Hebrew word, Hashem. It refers primarily to the sacred tetra grammaton the four-letter YHWH which to the best of our ability we pronounce it as Yahweh.

[01:29] And in Exodus 3, God reveals himself to Moses and he uses this same Hebrew word Hashem and he says I am. It signifies God's self-existence, his covenant faithfulness and supreme authority. But often times he is simply called the name in English. It's almost like his actual name, if he has one, isn't all that important. But what is important are his attributes. But all the names listed in the Bible are about his attributes and how he relates to us. We do have a name for the son of God. He became a man and he was given a name just like everybody else.

[01:59] In our modern-day English translation, we use the name Jesus. I don't think it's wrong to call him that, nor any of the older versions of it. I don't think it matters what you call God as long as it aligns with one of his attributes. What is he to you? Is he a father, a redeemer, a savior, a provider, a healer? Is he the prince of peace or the king of kings? Now, I wouldn't simply call him God cuz that is definitely not his name. It's more of a title. But there are many gods, so you want to be specific and give him an attribute.

It was a problem during the Tower of Babel times when God distributed to the nations gods over them.
